## 1. Purpose

This procedure describes the grinding and homogenization of dried soil,
sediment, plant tissue, and other solid environmental samples to
produce a fine, uniform powder suitable for chemical, elemental, and
isotopic analysis. Many analytical methods require a homogeneous
subsample of 0.5--20 mg (e.g., EA-IRMS capsules,
[SOP-L414](SOP-L414-soil-ea-irms.qmd)) or 0.5--1.0 g (e.g., acid
digestion, [SOP-L410](SOP-L410-hotplate-acid-digestion.qmd),
[SOP-L411](SOP-L411-mars-microwave-digestion.qmd)). Without thorough
grinding and homogenization, small subsamples drawn from an
incompletely mixed bulk sample may not represent the true composition
of that sample, introducing analytical error unrelated to the
instrument or method [@Nelson1996; @Bremner1996]. Particle-size
reduction to $\leq$ 150 $\mu$m also improves combustion completeness
in high-temperature elemental analyzers and reduces between-capsule
mass variance in EA-IRMS work [@Sollins1999; @thermo_flashea].


## 2. Scope

- **Applies to:** Dry grinding and homogenization of air-dried or
  oven-dried (60--105 °C) solid samples, including mineral soils,
  organic soils, sediments, dried plant tissue, compost, and biochar,
  using agate or steel mortar and pestle, ball mill, or mechanical
  grinder.
- **Does not apply to:** Wet grinding or homogenization of fresh
  tissue (cryogenic grinding for molecular biology applications);
  sieving-only sample preparation (see
  [SOP-F400](../field_sops/SOP-F400-soil-sampling.qmd) for 2 mm
  sieving); bead beating for DNA extraction (integral to
  [SOP-L700](SOP-L700-dna-extraction.qmd)); ball milling specifically
  for TC and EA-IRMS (see [SOP-L117](SOP-L117-ball-mill-soil-prep.qmd)).
- **Location:** EA Program laboratory, SGM 134.


## 3. Responsibilities

| Role              | Responsibility |
|:------------------|:---------------|
| Lab PI            | Approve SOP |
| Lab Manager       | Maintain grinding equipment, replace worn components |
| Trained Personnel | Grind and homogenize samples per this SOP |
| New Students      | Complete training before independent use |


## 4. Definitions

| Term | Definition |
|:-----|:-----------|
| **Grinding** | Mechanical size reduction of solid particles by impact, compression, or abrasion [@Bernhardt1994]. |
| **Homogenization** | Mixing and size reduction to produce a sample in which any subsample of a given mass has the same composition as any other subsample of that mass [@Nelson1996]. |
| **Particle size ($d_{50}$)** | Median particle diameter by mass; the most common target for soil analysis is 150 $\mu$m (U.S. No. 100 mesh sieve) [@Nelson1996]. |
| **Cross-contamination** | Transfer of material from a previously processed sample to a subsequent one via residue retained on grinding equipment surfaces [@Boutton1991]. |
| **Sacrificial subsample** | A small amount of the upcoming sample ground and discarded before collecting the analytical aliquot, to purge residual material from equipment surfaces [@Boutton1991]. |
| **Respirable crystalline silica (RCS)** | Quartz and cristobalite particles $\leq$ 10 $\mu$m aerodynamic diameter released during grinding of mineral soils; an IARC Group 1 carcinogen [@IARC1997]. |
| **Air-dried** | Dried at ambient temperature ($\leq$ 40 °C) until mass is constant; the standard pre-treatment for 2 mm sieving [@Nelson1996]. |


## 5. Safety and Hazards

::: {.callout-warning}
### Hazards

- **Respirable dust and silica:** Grinding dry soil and plant tissue
  generates fine respirable dust including crystalline silica (quartz),
  which is an IARC Group 1 carcinogen at particle sizes $\leq$ 10
  $\mu$m [@IARC1997]. Always perform grinding inside a fume hood or
  wear a NIOSH-approved N95 respirator.
- **Contaminated soils:** Soils from legacy-contaminated sites (Pb,
  As, Hg, pesticides, PAHs) pose additional inhalation and dermal
  hazards during grinding. Consult the Lab PI before processing
  [@USEPA3051A].
- **Noise:** Ball mills and mechanical grinders can exceed 85 dB.
  Wear hearing protection for runs $>$ 1 min [@NIOSH1998].
- **Pinch/crush hazards:** Ball mill jars and clamps are heavy.
  Secure jars before starting the mill and keep hands clear during
  operation.
- **Cross-contamination:** Residual sample in grinding equipment is
  the primary quality risk in sequential grinding. Thorough cleaning
  between samples is essential (Section 6.5).
:::

### Required PPE

- [ ] Safety glasses
- [ ] Lab coat
- [ ] Nitrile gloves
- [ ] N95 dust mask or work in fume hood
- [ ] Hearing protection (ball mill or mechanical grinder)

### Emergency Procedures

For dust inhalation, move to fresh air immediately. For cuts from
broken equipment, apply first aid per
[SOP-L002](SOP-L002-laboratory-safety.qmd). Report all incidents to
the Lab Manager.


## 6. Equipment and Materials

### 6.1 Grinding Equipment

| Item | Location | Best For |
|:-----|:---------|:---------|
| Agate mortar and pestle (various sizes) | SGM 134 | Small batches ($<$ 50 g); trace metal work (low contamination) |
| Ceramic (porcelain) mortar and pestle | SGM 134 | General purpose; not for trace metals (contributes Al, Si) |
| Ball mill (planetary or mixer mill) | SGM 134 | Large batches; consistent particle size; high throughput; see [SOP-L117](SOP-L117-ball-mill-soil-prep.qmd) for TC/EA-IRMS-specific protocol |
| Mechanical grinder (Wiley mill, Thomas mill) | TBD | Plant tissue; coarse initial grinding |

### 6.2 Accessories

| Item | Notes |
|:-----|:------|
| Stainless steel spatula | Transferring sample |
| Brush (soft bristle, nylon) | Cleaning mortar and mill jars |
| Lint-free wipes (Kimtech) | Wiping surfaces |
| 70% ethanol spray bottle | Decontamination |
| Compressed air (can or line) | Blowing dust from crevices |
| Test sieves (No. 60 = 250 $\mu$m; No. 100 = 150 $\mu$m; No. 200 = 75 $\mu$m) | Verifying particle size |
| Labeled sample vials or coin envelopes | Storing ground samples |
| Analytical balance | Per [SOP-L200](SOP-L200-analytical-balance-calibration.qmd) |


## 7. Procedure

### 7.1 Sample Selection and Drying

Samples must be thoroughly dry before grinding. Residual moisture
causes particles to clump, impedes size reduction, and can promote
microbial activity that alters sample chemistry during storage
[@Nelson1996].

1. Use air-dried samples sieved to 2 mm
   ([SOP-F400](../field_sops/SOP-F400-soil-sampling.qmd)), or
   oven-dry per the drying requirements in the table below:

   | Analytical Pathway | Drying Temperature | Rationale |
   |:-------------------|:------------------:|:----------|
   | TC, LOI, metals, or general chemistry | 105 °C to constant mass | Standard gravimetric drying; isotope fractionation not a concern [@Nelson1996] |
   | $\delta^{15}$N, $\delta^{13}$C (EA-IRMS) | 40--60 °C to constant mass | Temperatures $>$ 60 °C volatilize $^{14}$N-enriched NH$_4^+$, artificially elevating $\delta^{15}$N [@Kool2011; @Guntiñas2012] |
   | Plant tissue (any analysis) | 60 °C to constant mass | Higher temperatures degrade labile N compounds and alter tissue $\delta^{15}$N [@Kalra1998] |

2. Cool samples to room temperature in a desiccator before grinding.
3. Record drying temperature, start and end times, and initial and
   final mass in the lab notebook.

### 7.2 Mortar and Pestle (Manual Grinding)

Manual grinding with mortar and pestle is appropriate for small
batches ($<$ 50 g), hard materials requiring careful size control,
and laboratories where a ball mill is unavailable [@Nelson1996].

1. Place a clean, dry mortar on a stable bench surface. If working
   with contaminated soil or generating visible dust, work inside a
   fume hood.
2. Add a small amount of dried sample (5--20 g) to the mortar.
3. Grind with a circular and pressing motion, periodically scraping
   material from the sides back to the center.
4. Continue grinding until the sample passes through the target sieve
   (No. 60 [250 $\mu$m] for general chemistry; No. 100 [150 $\mu$m]
   for EA-IRMS [@thermo_flashea]). For plant tissue, grind to a
   uniform fine powder.
5. Transfer the ground sample to a labeled vial or coin envelope with
   a clean spatula.
6. Record the sample ID and particle size achieved.

::: {.callout-tip}
For hard or fibrous samples (e.g., woody roots, calcium carbonate
nodules), pre-crush coarsely with a hammer inside a thick plastic bag
before transferring to the mortar. This reduces grinding time and wear
on the mortar.
:::

### 7.3 Ball Mill (Mechanical Grinding)

Ball milling provides more reproducible particle size reduction and
higher throughput than manual grinding, and is preferred for batches
$>$ 20 samples or where particle size uniformity is critical
[@Bernhardt1994]. For samples destined for TC (Shimadzu SSM-5000A)
or EA-IRMS ($\delta^{15}$N, $\delta^{13}$C), follow the
instrument-specific protocol in
[SOP-L117](SOP-L117-ball-mill-soil-prep.qmd) instead.

1. Select the appropriate grinding jar and ball material:

   | Material | Best Use Case | Notes |
   |:---------|:--------------|:------|
   | Agate | Trace metal work | Low contamination; chips if used with coarse hard samples |
   | Stainless steel | General chemistry (non-metal) | Faster; may contribute Fe, Cr, Ni, Mn |
   | Zirconia (ZrO$_2$) | C/N/isotopes | Hard, chemically inert; preferred for EA-IRMS [@harris2001] |
   | Tungsten carbide | Hard minerals | Avoid for carbon analysis; W contributes to combustion gas |

2. Load the sample into the jar (no more than one-third of jar volume
   to allow ball movement).
3. Add grinding balls per the manufacturer's recommendation (typically
   1:10 ball-to-sample mass ratio for a planetary mill
   [@Bernhardt1994]).
4. Secure the jar in the mill clamp and close the lid.
5. Set speed and duration per the table below or per the analytical
   SOP:

   | Sample Type | Speed (rpm) | Duration | Target Size |
   |:------------|:-----------:|:--------:|:-----------:|
   | Mineral soil | 300--400 | 5--10 min | $\leq$ 150 $\mu$m |
   | Organic soil | 200--300 | 3--5 min | $\leq$ 250 $\mu$m |
   | Dried plant tissue | 200--300 | 2--5 min | fine powder |
   | Sediment | 300--400 | 5--10 min | $\leq$ 150 $\mu$m |

6. Run the mill. If the jar becomes warm to the touch, alternate
   2-minute grinding intervals with 1-minute rest periods to prevent
   thermal alteration of labile organic matter and N compounds
   [@Kool2011].
7. Wait 30 seconds after stopping before opening the jar (dust
   settles). Open inside the fume hood or with N95 protection.
8. Transfer the ground sample to a labeled container.
9. If required, verify particle size by passing a subsample through
   the target sieve.

### 7.4 Mechanical Grinder (Plant Tissue)

A Wiley-type or Thomas-type cutting mill provides rapid coarse
grinding of dried plant tissue and is generally faster than mortar
and pestle for batch processing [@Kalra1998].

1. Set the screen mesh to the target particle size (1 mm [No. 18]
   or 0.5 mm [No. 35]).
2. Feed dried tissue into the hopper slowly; do not overload.
3. Collect ground material from the output chamber.
4. For analyses requiring finer particle size (e.g., EA-IRMS), follow
   with mortar and pestle or ball mill to reduce further
   [@thermo_flashea].

### 7.5 Cleaning Between Samples

Cross-contamination is the primary quality risk in sequential grinding.
For isotope work, residues as small as 0.05 mg C from a high-carbon
sample can produce measurable $\delta^{13}$C bias in a subsequent
low-carbon sample [@Boutton1991]. Clean thoroughly between every
sample:

1. Disassemble the mortar/pestle or mill jar and balls.
2. Brush out all visible residue with a soft-bristle brush.
3. Wipe all surfaces with a lint-free tissue dampened with 70%
   ethanol.
4. **Trace metal work:** rinse with 10% HNO$_3$ (trace-metal grade),
   then triple-rinse with Type I deionized water (18.2 M$\Omega$), and
   air-dry [@USEPA3051A].
5. **Isotope work:** rinse with Type I deionized water, wipe with
   ethanol, and blow dry with clean compressed air.
6. **Wiley mill:** run a small amount of clean quartz sand through the
   mill between samples to abrade residues from the cutting chamber,
   then brush and wipe.
7. Allow all equipment to dry completely before grinding the next
   sample.

::: {.callout-important}
When transitioning between samples with very different compositions
(e.g., high-carbon compost followed by low-carbon mineral soil),
grind a sacrificial subsample of the next sample and discard it before
collecting the analytical aliquot. This purges micro-residues that
ethanol-wiping alone may not remove [@Boutton1991]. This step is
mandatory for EA-IRMS work.
:::

### 7.6 Storage

1. Transfer ground powder to a labeled vial (glass or polypropylene
   with a polyethylene-lined cap). Avoid foam-gasketed caps, which
   can off-gas organic vapors.
2. Label with: sample ID, date ground, equipment and jar material,
   and target particle size.
3. Store in a desiccator at room temperature. Ground samples have
   large surface area and are hygroscopic; even brief exposure to
   humid air can add 0.5--2% mass as adsorbed water [@Nelson1996].
4. For long-term storage ($>$ 2 weeks), seal with Parafilm and store
   at $-$20 °C.
5. Record grinding date, equipment, jar material, speed, and duration
   in the lab notebook and sample tracking spreadsheet.


## 8. Quality Control

| QC Check | Frequency | Acceptance Criterion |
|:---------|:---------:|:---------------------|
| Particle size verification (sieve) | $\geq$ 10% of samples per batch | $\geq$ 90% by mass passes target sieve; re-grind failures |
| Equipment blank (clean jar milled 2 min) | Once per batch and after new jar | No visible powder; TC blank $<$ 0.05 mg C if applicable |
| Certified reference material (CRM) -- trace metals | 1 per batch (trace metal work) | Recovered elemental concentration within 10% of certified value [@USEPA3051A] |
| Reference standard -- isotopes (USGS40, USGS41a) | 1 per batch (isotope work) | $\delta^{13}$C within $\pm$ 0.5 \textperthousand{}; $\delta^{15}$N within $\pm$ 0.5 \textperthousand{} of certified value [@brand2014] |
| Sample replicate (duplicate grind) | 1 per 10 samples | %C or %N: CV $\leq$ 5%; isotopes: SD $\leq$ 0.3 \textperthousand{} |
| Sacrificial subsample log | Every inter-sample cleaning (isotope work) | Recorded in lab notebook |

Document grinding equipment and jar material for every batch; different
materials introduce different trace elements and the record is
essential for troubleshooting contamination [@Bernhardt1994].


## 9. Waste Disposal

| Waste Type | Disposal Method |
|:-----------|:----------------|
| Grinding residue (non-hazardous soil/plant) | Standard solid waste or return to sample stock |
| Grinding residue (contaminated soil) | Hazardous solid waste per [SOP-L006](SOP-L006-waste-disposal.qmd) |
| Quartz sand (cleaning aid) | Standard solid waste |
| Used ethanol wipes | Standard solid waste (non-halogenated) |
| Worn grinding balls or jars (agate, ceramic) | Standard solid waste |
| Worn grinding components (stainless steel) | Metal recycling |
| HNO$_3$ rinse waste | Acid waste per [SOP-L006](SOP-L006-waste-disposal.qmd) |

## 12. Training Record

Before grinding samples independently, personnel must:

1. Read this SOP in full and sign the SOP acknowledgment form.
2. Complete [SOP-L002 Laboratory Safety](SOP-L002-laboratory-safety.qmd)
   training.
3. Demonstrate proper mortar-and-pestle technique including grinding
   motion and inter-sample cleaning.
4. If using the ball mill, demonstrate proper jar loading, speed/time
   selection, and jar cleaning per Section 7.5.
5. Grind at least 5 samples under supervision with acceptable particle
   size verification (all material passes the target sieve).
6. Be signed off by the PI or Lab Manager.
